notes: Estimand: the effect of being prescribed antipsychotic medication, versus not being prescribed it, on working at the 20-year follow-up, in a naturalistic non-randomised comparison. The two counts (9 of 36 and 16 of 22) exist in the report only as the two sides of that comparison, which is why ROBINS-I rather than the JBI prevalence checklist is applied: neither count is a whole-cohort prevalence, and neither arm was randomised. This row is the 'prescribed antipsychotics at 20 years' side. Medication status was determined by clinicians and patients, not by the investigators, so confounding by indication is intrinsic: patients who remain on antipsychotics for twenty years differ systematically in illness severity, insight and treatment engagement from those who stop, and the report itself shows that those continuously prescribed antipsychotics were significantly more likely to have negative symptoms, which it also shows predicts not working. The authors address this seriously, with separate analyses controlling for prognostic potential (Vaillant), premorbid developmental achievement (Zigler), psychosis and negative symptoms, and a GEE logistic and proportional-odds model adjusting for prognosis, premorbid functioning and symptoms. Those adjustments are post-hoc, use dichotomised covariates, and cannot address baseline severity determining both medication continuation and work capacity. The specific 20-year comparison reported as 9/36 v. 16/22 is unadjusted. Independent AI verification; does not satisfy a named human/non-author verification requirement. Applicability: these stored arm-specific counts are not themselves a comparative effect estimate; tool judgement applies provisionally to the source comparison and cannot certify whole-cohort prevalence eligibility.
